title: About
text:
Shelby Slein
Welcome to my NCAA Division 1 Volleyball analytics project!
This website examines individual player performance from 2020 through 2026, investigating how experience level and class standing relate to scoring output, attacking efficiency, and defensive impact.
The data for this project was sourced from official NCAA Statistics spanning the 2020 through 2026 seasons. You can also view and download the compiled dataset directly from the GitHub project data repository.

title: Comparing Volleyball Stats by Class Year
text: We analyze whether collegiate experience level (Freshman, Sophomore, Junior, Senior) in NCAA Division 1 volleyball impacts player performance across multiple facets of the game: scoring, attacking efficiency, setting, serving, and defense.

title: Comparing Volleyball Stats by Class Year
text:
Key Takeaways

Overall Scoring: Average points per set increases by 39% from Freshman year (1.28) to Senior year (1.78).
Attacking Volume & Efficiency: Seniors average 1.39 kills per set with a .185 average hitting percentage, compared to 0.98 kills per set and .141 hitting percentage for freshmen.
Net Defense: Average blocks per set climb from 0.28 (freshmen) to 0.37 (seniors), a 32% increase.
Floor Defense: Digs per set increase steadily each year, rising from 1.20 to 1.53 per set.

title: Background
text: In NCAA Division 1 women’s volleyball, athletes face steep competition and rigorous physical demands. A key question in sports analytics is how much court experience and physical maturation across collegiate eligibility translate into measurable statistical gains.

title: Background
text:
Research Motivation
Do upperclassmen (juniors and seniors) consistently outperform underclassmen (freshmen and sophomores), and in which facets of the game—scoring volume, attacking discipline, net defense, or floor defense—is that advantage most pronounced?

title: Does Experience Affect College Volleyball Performance?
text:
In collegiate athletics, players often improve as they progress through their college careers. But does experience level substantially affect individual volleyball statistics?
To answer this question, we collected comprehensive individual season statistics across six seasons of NCAA Division 1 women’s volleyball (2020–2026), covering over 31,000 player-seasons across four class standings:

Freshmen (Fr)
Sophomores (So)
Juniors (Jr)
Seniors (Sr)

title: Does Experience Affect College Volleyball Performance?
text:
Core Findings
As players progress from freshman to senior year:

Total Scoring: Seniors average 1.78 points per set, compared to 1.28 for freshmen (+39%).
Attacking Volume & Efficiency: Seniors average 1.39 kills per set with a .185 average hitting percentage, compared to 0.98 kills per set and .141 hitting percentage for freshmen.
Net Defense: Blocks per set increase from 0.28 (freshmen) to 0.37 (seniors) (+32%).
Floor Defense: Digs per set increase from 1.20 (freshmen) to 1.53 (seniors) (+28%).
Serving & Setting: Service aces and assists also rise as players take on expanded rotation duties.

Explore the interactive charts, summary tables, and player explorer on the Stats Comparison page.

title: The Veteran Advantage: Learning to Win at the Net
text:
When evaluating collegiate volleyball attackers, raw kill totals often grab headlines. But in high-level NCAA Division 1 play, rallies frequently hinge on attacking discipline: putting the ball to the floor without handing free points to the opponent on unforced errors. To understand how collegiate hitters mature, we examined individual season statistics from over 15,000 player-seasons across six NCAA seasons (2020–2026), filtering for active attackers with at least 100 attack attempts.
The data reveals a steady, two-sided evolution. As attackers progress from their freshman to senior campaigns, their kill rate climbs monotonically from 34.5% to 36.9%. At the same time, their attack error rate declines each year, dropping from 16.4% down to 14.3%. Together, these compounding adjustments explain why seniors hit at an average efficiency of .226 compared to .181 for freshmen: veterans generate more offensive points while donating fewer errors.

title: The Veteran Advantage: Learning to Win at the Net
section: Position Breakdown: Outside Hitters vs. Middle Blockers
text:
Position Breakdown: Outside Hitters vs. Middle Blockers
Not all hitting roles are created equal. Middle Blockers (MB) attack quick sets close to the setter, often facing single blockers, while Outside Hitters (OH) carry the burden of out-of-system “bailout” sets against formed double blocks. Does collegiate experience help both roles equally?









The split shows that experience pays off differently depending on the role. Middle Blockers maintain high kill rates from day one (39.5% as freshmen) because of their physical height and set speed, yet they still trim errors down from 15.5% to 13.7%. Outside Hitters experience an even more noticeable transformation: their error rate drops by more than two full points (17.4% to 15.2%) while kill rates jump from 32.3% to 34.0%, demonstrating how seasoned pins learn to manage difficult balls.

title: The Veteran Advantage: Learning to Win at the Net
text:
Case Study: Marta Levinska (Arizona State)
Aggregate statistics show broad patterns, but individual careers bring the trend to life. Marta Levinska arrived at Arizona State in 2020 as a high-potential international opposite/outside hitter. Over four consecutive seasons, her trajectory tracked the veteran curve with textbook precision.









As a freshman, Levinska delivered a productive 245 kills with a .204 hitting percentage. By her senior campaign in 2023–24, she racked up 571 kills while pushing her kill rate to 45.8% and cutting her error rate to 11.0%—earning AVCA All-America honors and guiding Arizona State to the NCAA Sweet 16. Her growth exemplifies how collegiate attackers combine strength, shot selection, and court vision to dominate at the net.

title: Player Journey
text:
Over the past few years of watching college volleyball, I have become increasingly interested in the statistics behind the players. Specifically, the way in which experience affects overall production of points over the course of a player’s career. Every year there are freshman stars and then there are those players that continue to steadily improve and grow.
I began to think about how each year there are steady improvements in players’ stats all around. I have played volleyball for most of my life, so, seeing how each rep can make you better seemed to stop once you reached the highest collegiate level in my mind. Before researching this topic, I saw lots in the media about comparison to a player’s stats from the previous year to now, how it could be their breakout year, or how they could fall into a slump. So, I began to research if the past years’ stats could predict an increase in overall point production per player.

title: Player Journey
text:
The Evidence in the Data
Using statistics from the past six seasons from the official NCAA, I began to see an upward trend in how each player can still grow at one of the highest levels. In each category—points per set, kills, errors, and more—there were significant findings that showcased the improvement in each player’s game, whether they were a star since freshman year or someone who rarely saw playing time.

title: Player Journey
text:
Case Study: Marta Levinska (Arizona State)
In my data, I decided to conduct a case study revolving around one player specifically. Marta Levinska from Arizona State played all four years and was a breakout star in her freshman campaign back in 2020. In her four years, not only did she grow, but she also improved her point production rate by over 12 percent, which is significantly high.

title: Player Journey
text:
Impact for Athletes and Coaches
The broad data gathered and case study can be very helpful and reassuring to younger athletes and those already in college. Those athletes that start to doubt the work they put in can now see that there is statistical proof showcasing that the work they put in is working and pushing them to be the best athlete they can be.
Another group that could find interest in this data is the coaches behind these high-level teams. Seeing that even the unranked and lower recruits on a list can be just as effective as the number one recruits in the nation by their sophomore year can throw the entire recruiting process for a loop.
